sentences.text: Spinosaurus mirabilis possessed a distinctive pointed crest formed by the nasal and prefrontal bones that resembled a scimitar.
The crest rose about 50 cm above the skull roof and was likely covered in keratin, suggesting a role in visual display or recognition among individuals.
The holotype, a subadult, measured roughly 8 m in total length, while researchers estimate that fully mature individuals could have reached 10 to 14 m.
Spinosaurus mirabilis is placed within the spinosaurid theropods, specifically in the family Spinosauridae, subfamily Spinosaurinae, and tribe Spinosaurini.
Its 50 cm high crest is the tallest known bony ornament among spinosaurids.
The species lived in an interior basin of the central Sahara, far from coastal environments where other spinosaurids are known.
The holotype’s length of 8 m makes it one of the smallest known members of the genus Spinosaurus.
Fossils of Spinosaurus mirabilis were collected in Niger during excavations in 2000, 2019, and 2022 under the direction of Paul Sereno.
Specimens came from two localities, Iguidi and Jenguebi, within the Farak Formation.
The most diagnostic material, recovered from Jenguebi between 2019 and 2022, formed the basis of the species description published in Science on 19 February 2026.
Since its description, the Jenguebi fossils have been stored at Abdou Moumouni University in Niger, while the Iguidi material is on loan to Sereno’s laboratory at the University of Chicago.
The occurrence of S. mirabilis in fluvial sandstone and sandy shale indicates a riparian habitat preference.
It is interpreted as a wading hunter that could move through shallow water to ambush aquatic prey along river margins.
Phylogenetic analysis recovers Spinosaurus mirabilis as the sister taxon to Spinosaurus aegyptiacus, placing it within the parent group Spinosaurus.
The species belongs to the class Reptilia.
Spinosaurus mirabilis lived during the Cenomanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, about 95 million years ago, within a fluvial system of the Farak Formation.
The Cenomanian age of its strata matches that of Spinosaurus aegyptiacus fossils elsewhere.
Researchers debate whether certain cervical vertebrae previously assigned to Carcharodontosaurus saharicus actually belong to a spinosaurid.
Interpretations of the species’ lifestyle have shifted between viewing it as a semi-aquatic ambush predator and a fully aquatic diver.
Some scientists propose that spinosaurid evolution proceeded in three discrete phases, a hypothesis that includes S. mirabilis.
